rich_summary: Returning from killing the demon Maricha, Rama is troubled by ominous signs and fears for Sita’s safety. When he reaches the forest hermitage and finds it deserted, dread turns to anguish. The once-beautiful dwelling appears lifeless, as if the forest itself mourns her absence. Rama frantically searches the woods, running across hills and streams, calling out to trees, animals, and the very landscape to reveal where Sita has gone. In his grief he imagines terrible possibilities—abduction, death, or being devoured by beasts. His desperate appeals and hallucinated glimpses of Sita show the depth of his love and despair. This chapter marks the emotional turning point after Sita’s abduction and launches the epic search that will shape the rest of the Ramayana.

highlight_spans.why: Rama recounts how the demon in the form of a deer deceived them, revealing the ruse that enabled Sita’s abduction.
Rama arrives at the deserted hermitage and realizes Sita is gone—the pivotal discovery that begins the desperate search.
Rama addresses the forest trees as witnesses, reflecting the epic’s animistic world where nature is treated as conscious and divine.
His grief intensifies as he imagines Sita dead or devoured, showing the emotional devastation behind the heroic quest.
Rama calls out desperately to Sita as if she were hiding nearby, a poignant moment revealing his near-mad desperation.

top_scenes.scene_text: Rama standing before the abandoned forest hermitage at dusk, the hut empty, flowers faded and animals silent, as he realizes Sita has vanished.
Rama wandering frantically through the forest, arms raised as he questions towering trees—Ashoka, Tala, and Jambu—while birds and deer watch in the dim green light.
Rama running through the wilderness like one possessed, calling Sita’s name among rivers, hills, and waterfalls while the vast forest surrounds him.
